title: AI as a teaching tool and learning partner
extended_summary:
This paper examines how large language model (LLM)-based AI tools can be integrated into higher education as supports for teaching and learning, with a focus on student attitudes, comfort, and perceived benefits. The authors position the work against a backdrop of concern about AI misuse in assessment and instead ask how AI might function constructively as a teaching tool and learning partner in Life Sciences courses.

The intervention involved introducing two AI-supported resources into two biology-related modules at Ulster University: a module-specific chatbot powered by an LLM and enhanced with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over course materials, and weekly AI-generated audio podcasts based on each week's teaching content. The chatbot was updated weekly with module materials such as lecture notes, handbook information, supplementary reading, assessment guidance, and rubrics, and students could use it for explanations, revision plans, and study aids. At the end of the semester, students were surveyed about their use of and attitudes toward these tools.

The population consisted of small undergraduate and postgraduate cohorts in biological sciences: BIO123 (BSc Personalised Medicine) and BIO711 (MSc Biotechnology). The study took place in a higher education setting at a single UK institution. From a total cohort of 41 students, 28 responses were received, with some incomplete. Results were primarily based on self-reported survey data about perceptions of AI, confidence using AI tools, and experiences with the chatbot and podcasts.

The main conclusions are that students were generally positive about AI and especially receptive to the module-specific chatbot, which they found easy and enjoyable to use and helpful for learning. The AI-generated podcasts were used less frequently and were less broadly endorsed, though students who did listen tended to value them. The authors conclude that there is clear student appetite for AI-supported learning tools, but that uneven confidence with AI suggests a need for support for both students and staff if such tools are to be integrated equitably and effectively.

identified_tools.name: Gemini
identified_tools.description: Google's family of large language models and related tooling used to build conversational assistants and generate content.
identified_tools.use_case: A Google-powered, module-specific LLM chatbot was deployed with retrieval-augmented access to course materials (module handbook, lecture notes, readings, assessment guidelines, rubrics) for two life sciences courses; it was used to answer student questions, provide alternative explanations, revision timetables, and flashcards. The same AI setup was also used to generate weekly audio-only podcasts based on teaching materials.

findings.finding_summary: Students reported a positive usability experience with the AI-powered chatbot. Agreement with “I found it easy to understand how to use the AI-chatbot” had a mean of 4.1 based on 24 responses, and agreement with “I enjoyed using the AI-chatbot” had a mean of 4.2 based on 24 responses.
findings.measure: Student survey ratings of chatbot ease of use and enjoyment (Likert-scale agreement)

findings.finding_summary: Perceived learning support from the chatbot was unanimously positive among respondents. 100% agreed that “Using the AI-chatbot enhanced my knowledge of the module learning content” based on 20 responses.
findings.measure: Student survey agreement that chatbot enhanced knowledge of module learning content

findings.finding_summary: AI-generated podcasts were less widely used than the chatbot: the majority of respondents used them occasionally or never, and few listened weekly (25 responses). Among students who listened at least occasionally, enjoyment was positive, with agreement on “I enjoyed listening to the AI-generated podcast” averaging 4.3 based on 15 responses.
findings.measure: Podcast usage frequency and student enjoyment survey ratings

findings.finding_summary: Interest in broader adoption of AI-generated podcasts was mixed overall but more positive among users. Across all responses, agreement with “I would like to see AI-generated podcasts made available in more of my modules” had a mean of 3.5 (22 responses), while among students who listened at least occasionally the mean was 4.1 (15 responses).
findings.measure: Student survey ratings on desire for wider podcast use

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI tools, including LLM-based learning supports and AI-generated multimedia resources, without a specific named product identified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper also reports students' attitudes toward AI tools overall and their perceived gains from using the AI-chatbot and AI-generated podcasts combined.

findings.finding_summary: Students were broadly positive about AI and its role in teaching and learning. Agreement with the statement that AI tools will make a positive or negative contribution to society (1=very negative, 5=very positive) had a mean of 4.0 based on 21 responses, and 75% agreed that they regularly use AI tools outside their courses based on 16 responses.
findings.measure: Student attitudes toward AI and self-reported AI use

findings.finding_summary: Students who responded reported perceived benefit from the AI tools provided in the courses. 100% agreed that “I do feel that I gained from using the AI-chatbots and AI-generated podcasts” based on 14 responses.
findings.measure: Student survey agreement on perceived gains from AI-chatbots and AI-generated podcasts

findings.finding_summary: Students appeared positive about AI but only moderately confident in their own AI skills. Self-rated AI skill level on a 1=poor to 5=high scale had a mean of 3.2 based on 21 responses.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a small-scale survey-based study of student attitudes and perceived benefits in two higher education classes, without randomization, control group, or objective learning outcome measures. The evidence is useful but primarily perceptual and exploratory.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are positive but based on self-reported satisfaction, enjoyment, and perceived learning rather than measured achievement gains, and no effect sizes are provided. Impact therefore appears promising but unclear in magnitude.
